content: 1. Psychosocial support should include, at a minimum, an assessment of psychosocial needs, supportive counseling, and connections to existing family and community services. Baseline levels must first be measured, and countries should set ambitious yet realistic targets to maximize the percentage of individuals on maintenance opioid substitution therapy (OST) who receive a minimum package of psychosocial support. 2. Community-based naloxone distribution sites should be identified and documented. These sites dispense naloxone to lay providers, including opioid users, their peers, and family members, for managing opioid overdoses. The number of such sites is a critical indicator for monitoring the scale-up of community-based naloxone distribution. Baseline levels should be measured, and countries should set realistic targets and timeframes for expanding naloxone distribution. 3. Sites providing safe injecting equipment for gender affirmation should be documented. These sites may include fixed services or mobile outreach locations serving transgender individuals. Not all transgender individuals inject substances for gender affirmation, but appropriate sites should be identified and equipped to meet their needs. Targets should be set for scaling up access to safe injecting equipment, considering logistical and resource requirements. 4. Behavioral interventions for sexual risk reduction should be provided at sites focused on key populations. The total number of such sites should be tracked, and targets should be set for increasing their availability over time. However, an increase in the number of sites does not necessarily equate to improved accessibility. Structured interventions requiring regular sessions may not be feasible through outreach services. 5. Brief intervention counseling for problematic substance use should be available at sites serving key populations. This evidence-based motivational counseling technique is effective in addressing drug and alcohol misuse. Countries should identify sites with the potential to provide such counseling and set targets for scaling up these services, ensuring appropriate training and resources are in place. 6. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention should be made available to men who have sex with men. Sites providing PrEP must be identified to collect relevant programmatic data. Baseline levels should be measured, and countries should set ambitious yet realistic targets and timeframes for scaling up PrEP access. 7. HIV testing and counseling (HTC) services should be available at sites meeting national quality standards. These sites may include fixed services or mobile outreach locations. Key population-focused programs and mainstream services meeting key population sensitivity standards should provide HTC without stigma or discrimination. Targets should be set for increasing the number of such sites, ensuring accessibility and acceptability for key populations. 8. Efforts should be made to ensure that individuals tested for HIV receive their results. The target for this indicator should be set at 100%. Baseline levels can be established through initial surveys, and countries should set realistic timeframes for increasing the proportion of tests for which results are provided. 9. Voluntary HTC should be available in prisons and other closed settings, but HIV testing should never be mandatory in any setting. Countries should set targets and timeframes for scaling up HTC services, ensuring they meet the needs of key populations and adhere to sensitivity standards. 10. UNAIDS has set ambitious 90:90:90 targets for scaling up antiretroviral treatment, including the goal that by 2020, 90% of all people living with HIV will know their HIV status. Integrated bio-behavioral surveys can provide insights into achieving this goal among key populations.
